blocks.text: The law concerning honey is found in Levit. II, 11. 12. No leaven and no honey shall you burn to God as an offering to be consumed by fire. As an offering of first fruits, however, you shall offer them to the Lord. But they shall not be offered upon the altar for a sweet savour. Here R. Selomo understands by the name of honey כל מתיקת פרי, all the sweetness of fruits, and some in Aben Ezra understand dates, as in 2 Paral. XXXI, 5., where the Israelites are said to have offered the first fruits of grain, must, oil and honey, and all the produce of the field. And indeed it will seem probable that Ezra means the same thing as is meant in the Law, since both passages deal with the first fruits of honey offered, or to be offered, to God. But if the Law were speaking of dates, or of the fruits of trees in general, the Law would nowhere have forbidden the use of honey in sacrifices. Yet all the ancients consistently teach that it was forbidden: among outside writers, Plutarch, book 4 of the Symposiaca, ch. 5; among the Jews, Philo, Περὶ θυόντων [Peri thyontōn]; from the choir of the Fathers, Jerome, Chrysostom, Procopius, Cyril, Theodoret, etc. So, whatever the more recent Hebrews may hold, I think that in both places the name דבש signifies honey, and that what is first gathered from the hives in springtime is called the first fruits of honey. Further, why the Law forbids honey to be offered on the altar, no one can easily say, and different people devise different reasons. Philo says honey is forbidden ἐπειδήπερ ἡ συναγωγὸς αὐτοῦ μέλιττα ζῶόν ἐστιν οὐ καθαρὸν, σήψεως καὶ φθορᾶς νεκρῶν, ὡς ὁ λόγος, βοῶν γεννώμενον [epeidēper hē synagōgos autou melitta zōon estin ou katharon, sēpseōs kai phthoras nekrōn, hōs ho logos, boōn gennōmenon], because its gatherer, the bee, is an impure animal, which they say is born from the putrefaction and corruption of dead oxen. Others, in Theodoret, say ὡς τῆς μελίττης καὶ ἀκαθάρτοις τόποις ἐφιζανούσης, καὶ πάντοθεν ἀθροιζούσης τῆς μελιττουργίας τὰς ἀφορμὰς [hōs tēs melittēs kai akathartois topois ephizanousēs, kai pantothen athroizousēs tēs melittourgias tas aphormas], because the bee settles in impure places and gathers the material for making honey from everywhere. Others, in the same author, say διδάσκεσθαι ἡμᾶς ἐξ οἰκείων πόνων τὰς θυσίας ἐπιτελεῖν, κατὰ τὴν τοῦ Σολομῶντος παραίνεσιν· ὁ δὲ τῆς μελίττης καρπὸς, οὐχ ἡμέτερός φασι πόνος [didaskesthai hēmas ex oikeiōn ponōn tas thysias epitelein, kata tēn tou Solomōntos parainesin; ho de tēs melittēs karpos, ouch hēmeteros phasi ponos], that we are taught by this that sacrifices must be paid from our own labours; but the fruit of the bee, as they say, does not come from our labour. He himself thinks that διὰ τοῦ μέλιτος τὴν ἡδονὴν ἀπαγορεύεσθαι [dia tou melitos tēn hēdonēn apagoreuesthai], under the name of honey pleasure is forbidden. This you may also read in Philo. And Jerome, in the ninth letter, to Eustochium, says that honey is not offered in the sacrifices of God, because with God nothing voluptuous, [col. 529] nothing merely sweet, is pleasing, unless it contains something of biting truth. And in the twelfth letter, to Gaudentius, to teach that one must abstain from the allurements of the flesh, he says: In the sacrifices of the Lord they do not offer honey; and, wax being despised, which is the lodging of honey, oil is lit in the temple of God, which is pressed out of the bitterness of olives. And Isychius on this passage wants it to be understood as the doctrine of the pagans, on account of the sweetness of their words and the charm of their eloquence. These views, though rather uncertain, can be [III, 394] tolerated. But it is laughable that Plutarch, while trying to prove that the Jews worshipped Bacchus, adduces among other things this, in book 4 of the Symposiaca, question 5: Ἔτι τοίνυν μέλι μὲν οὐ προσφέρουσι ταῖς ἱερουργίαις, ὅτι δοκεῖ φθείρειν τὸν οἶνον κεραννύμενον [Eti toinyn meli men ou prospherousi tais hierourgiais, hoti dokei phtheirein ton oinon kerannymenon]· Further, they do not offer honey in sacrifices, because when mixed with wine it seems to spoil it. As if they feared to provoke Bacchus by tainting wine with a mixture of honey. This reason is most absurd. For they could have offered wine and honey to Bacchus separately. Nor did this scruple affect the true worshippers of Bacchus, who offered him not only wine but also honey. The matter is certain from Tibullus, who addresses Bacchus thus in book 1, Elegy 8:
So may you come today: to you I would give the honours of incense, and bring cakes sweet with Mopsopian honey.
Cakes are made for the god, because he delights in sweet juices, and they say honey was discovered by Bacchus.

Hence his name Brisaeus, as we noted above. But that honey was also commonly offered to other gods, there is no one who does not know. This God reproaches the Jewish congregation with in chapter 16 of Ezekiel: You made for yourself male images, he says, to play the harlot with them, etc. And my food which I had given you, fine flour, and oil, and honey, with which I had fed you, this you offered to them for a sweet savour. For there was hardly any of the gods to whom libation was not made with honey. Thus Antipater of Sidon says of Mercury, book 1 of the Anthology, chapter 38:
Εὔκολος Ἑρμείας, ὦ ποιμένες, ἐν δὲ γάλακτι Χαίρων, καὶ δρυΐνῳ σπενδόμενος μέλιτι· [Eukolos Hermeias, ō poimenes, en de galakti Chairōn, kai dryinō spendomenos meliti]
Easy to please is Mercury, O shepherds, who delights in milk and is appeased with oak honey. And Silius of Pluto, book 13, verse 415:
Bring with you the foretold appeasements for the sacred rites of harsh Dis, honey too, and carry the gifts of pure Lyaeus.
And Apollonius of Hecate, book 3 of the Argonautica, verse 1034.
